title: Pre-LN vs Post-LN, warmup, and the identity highway
text:
Post-LN (x_{l+1} = LN(x_l + Sub(x_l))): every backward gradient must pass through every LayerNorm Jacobian in the stack, in sequence. That Jacobian zeroes the gradient’s component along the mean direction, zeroes the component along the (x-μ)/σ direction (scale invariance), and shrinks whatever’s left by ≤ 1/σ. Multiply N of these together and you get exponential gradient shrinkage with depth — subspaces that survive one layer’s projection can get killed by the next.
Loss → [J_LN] → [J_LN] → [J_LN] → ... → [J_LN] → Early layer weights
        Layer N   Layer N-1                 Layer 1
        (shrinks) (shrinks again)          (barely anything left)
Pre-LN (x_{l+1} = x_l + Sub(LN(x_l))): the residual x_l is added outside the LN, so
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_l} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_{l+1}} \cdot \left(I + J_{\text{Sub}} \cdot J_{\text{LN}}\right)\]
The identity term I is a direct gradient highway: a copy of the output gradient reaches every layer untouched, no matter what the sublayer Jacobian does to the other term.
Loss
 │
 ├─────────────────────── Identity highway ──────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                    │
[Sub·LN Jacobian] → [Sub·LN Jacobian] → ... → [Sub·LN Jacobian]      │
                                                                      │
                                                        Early weights ←┘


Because Post-LN gradients shrink with depth, different layers have wildly different gradient magnitudes at any given step — a single global LR has to serve all of them at once:



Learning rate
Late layers
Early layers




Too high
Explode → divergence
Still okay


Too low
Learn slowly
Learn essentially nothing


Just right
Marginal stability
Still barely learning



There is no single LR that keeps late layers stable and gives early layers a usable signal — this is precisely why the original paper needs a warmup schedule as a bandage (more on that in §11). Pre-LN’s identity highway keeps gradient magnitude roughly uniform across depth, so one LR works comfortably almost everywhere, and higher LRs become tolerable.
The trade-off: Pre-LN’s residual stream grows unboundedly in the forward pass (nothing renormalizes it layer to layer), which is exactly why Encoder and Decoder each end with one more LayerNormalisation() after the last block — a final cleanup norm that Post-LN doesn’t strictly need, since Post-LN already renormalizes at every layer.
class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layers: nn.ModuleList):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers=layers
        self.norm=LayerNormalisation()   # <- the Pre-LN "final cleanup" norm
    
    def forward(self, x: Tensor, mask: Tensor=None):
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, mask)
        return self.norm(x)
That final self.norm(x) isn’t decorative — it’s the tell that confirms this implementation committed to Pre-LN, and it’s required for Pre-LN to work correctly.
Code

1. Introduction
Most people’s first contact with a Transformer these days is nn.TransformerEncoderLayer or a HuggingFace AutoModel. That’s the right call for shipping something — but it also means the internals stay a black box: the exact place dropout gets applied, why embeddings get scaled by √d_model, why the original paper’s learning rate schedule looks the way it does. This post is the opposite exercise: build the encoder-decoder Transformer from “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al., 2017) layer by layer, in plain PyTorch, and then use that implementation to actually test one of the architecture’s most consequential — and most under-explained — design choices: Pre-LN vs Post-LN, crossed with flat learning rate vs warmup+decay.
Scope: this is the original encoder-decoder machine-translation-style Transformer, not a decoder-only GPT-style model. That distinction matters later when we talk about cross-attention and masking.
By the end, you’ll have: - A full from-scratch implementation with every shape and design decision explained - A working mental model for why Pre-LN training is more stable than Post-LN - Empirical evidence (not just folklore) for how LR schedule interacts with normalization placement
This is the first post in a longer series — the next stops are KV caching, quantization (TurboQuant), and flow-matching-based generative models (DiT, F5-TTS), so I’ve tried to write the attention and masking sections in a way that will still be useful when we get to autoregressive decoding with a cache.

2. Architecture Overview
The Transformer is an encoder-decoder stack. The encoder maps an input sequence to a sequence of contextualized representations; the decoder generates an output sequence autoregressively, attending both to its own previous outputs (self-attention) and to the encoder’s output (cross-attention).
Input tokens → Embedding + PosEnc → [Encoder Layer × N] → Encoder Output
                                                                  │
Output tokens (shifted) → Embedding + PosEnc → [Decoder Layer × N] → Linear → Softmax
                                                        ▲
                                                        └── cross-attends to Encoder Output
Each encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network. Each decoder layer has three: masked multi-head self-attention, multi-head cross-attention over the encoder output, then feed-forward. Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization.

3. Input Representations

3.1 Token Embeddings and the √d_model Scale
Token IDs are mapped to d_model-dimensional vectors via a standard embedding table. The paper multiplies the embedding output by √d_model before adding positional encoding:
class InputEmbeddings(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, vocab_size: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.embedding(x) * math.sqrt(self.d_model)
Why scale at all? The embedding table is typically initialized with small variance (roughly unit variance per dimension under standard init), while the sinusoidal positional encoding has values bounded in [-1, 1] with a specific frequency structure. Without scaling, the positional signal — which is fixed and not learned — would dominate the token embedding at initialization, and the model would have to spend early training just “fighting” the positional signal to extract token identity. Scaling by √d_model roughly matches the two signals’ magnitudes so gradients flow through both proportionally from step one. This is a paper-idiosyncratic choice; many later architectures (like GPT-2) drop this scaling because they use learned positional embeddings initialized at a compatible scale to begin with.


3.2 Sinusoidal Positional Encoding
class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, seq_len: int, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        pe = torch.zeros(seq_len, d_model)
        position = torch.arange(0, seq_len, dtype=torch.float).unsqueeze(1)
        div_term = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() * (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model))
        pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * div_term)
        pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * div_term)
        pe = pe.unsqueeze(0)
        self.register_buffer('pe', pe)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.pe[:, :x.shape[1], :].requires_grad_(False)
        return self.dropout(x)
Why sin/cos instead of a learned positional embedding table? Two reasons the paper gives, and one practical one:

Extrapolation: sinusoidal encodings are defined for any position, so the model can in principle handle sequences longer than anything seen during training (in practice this generalization is weak, but it’s non-zero, whereas a learned embedding table simply has no vector for position 513 if trained on length-512 sequences).
Relative position as a linear function: for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be expressed as a linear transformation of PE(pos). This is because sin(a+b) and cos(a+b) expand into linear combinations of sin(a), cos(a), sin(b), cos(b). That means the model has an easy analytic handle for learning to attend by relative position, not just absolute position, if it’s useful for the task.
No extra parameters — a genuinely minor but real practical benefit.

The div_term construction is the standard log-space trick to compute 10000^(2i/d_model) for each dimension pair without numerical overflow — take the log, scale, exponentiate.

4. Attention Mechanism

4.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention
def attention(query, key, value, mask=None, dropout: nn.Dropout = None):
    d_k = query.shape[-1]
    attention_scores = (query @ key.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(d_k)
    if mask is not None:
        attention_scores.masked_fill_(mask == 0, -1e9)
    attention_scores = attention_scores.softmax(dim=-1)
    if dropout is not None:
        attention_scores = dropout(attention_scores)
    return (attention_scores @ value), attention_scores
Why divide by √d_k? Assume query and key components are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. The dot product q·k = Σ(q_i × k_i) over d_k terms has variance that grows linearly with d_k (variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of variances, and each term q_i·k_i has variance 1 under these assumptions). So the raw dot product has variance ≈ d_k, meaning its typical magnitude grows with √d_k. Large-magnitude inputs to softmax push it into saturated regions where the gradient is near zero almost everywhere except at the max — the softmax becomes nearly a hard argmax and gradients vanish for all the non-selected positions. Dividing by √d_k renormalizes the dot product back to unit variance regardless of d_k, keeping softmax in a well-conditioned regime.
Masking: masked_fill_(mask == 0, -1e9) happens before softmax, not after. Setting scores to a large negative number (rather than zero) ensures that after softmax, those positions get a weight of essentially exp(-1e9) ≈ 0 — masking after softmax would just leave the wrong probabilities in place and require manual renormalization.


4.2 Multi-Head Attention
class MultiHeadAttentionBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, h: int, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.h = h
        assert d_model % h == 0, "d_model must be divisible by h"
        self.d_k = d_model // h
        self.w_q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.w_k = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.w_v = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.w_o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, q, k, v, mask):
        query = self.w_q(q)
        key = self.w_k(k)
        value = self.w_v(v)

        # (batch, seq_len, d_model) -> (batch, h, seq_len, d_k)
        query = query.view(query.shape[0], query.shape[1], self.h, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        key = key.view(key.shape[0], key.shape[1], self.h, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)
        value = value.view(value.shape[0], value.shape[1], self.h, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2)

        x, self.attention_scores = attention(query, key, value, mask, self.dropout)

        # (batch, h, seq_len, d_k) -> (batch, seq_len, d_model)
        x = x.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(x.shape[0], -1, self.h * self.d_k)
        return self.w_o(x)
The key implementation gotcha here is the reshape sequence. Projecting to d_model and then viewing it as (h, d_k) — rather than running h separate smaller linear layers — is mathematically equivalent but dramatically more efficient: it’s one big matmul instead of h small ones, which matters a lot for GPU utilization. The .contiguous() call before the final .view() is not optional — .transpose() returns a view with non-contiguous memory layout, and .view() requires contiguous memory, so skipping this raises a runtime error (or silently wrong behavior if you use .reshape() instead, which will implicitly copy).
Why multiple heads at all, rather than one d_model-dimensional attention? Splitting into h heads of dimension d_k = d_model/h lets each head learn to attend using a different projection subspace — empirically, different heads specialize (some track short-range syntactic relations, others longer-range or positional patterns). A single full-size attention head, by contrast, is forced to average all such patterns into one attention distribution per query.

6. Residual Connections & Normalization
class ResidualConnection(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.norm = LayerNormalization()

    def forward(self, x, sublayer):
        return x + self.dropout(sublayer(self.norm(x)))  # Pre-LN
        # Post-LN alternative: return self.norm(x + self.dropout(sublayer(x)))

6.1 Post-LN vs Pre-LN
The original paper uses Post-LN: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). Normalization is applied after the residual addition, on the combined output.
Pre-LN instead normalizes the input to the sublayer, and adds the raw (unnormalized) sublayer output to the residual stream: x + Sublayer(LayerNorm(x)).
The practical difference is about gradient flow through depth. In Post-LN, every residual addition is immediately followed by a normalization that rescales the combined signal — this means the identity path (the raw residual x) gets its scale altered at every single layer, and gradients backpropagating through N stacked layers pass through N layer-norm rescalings, each of which can shrink or distort gradient magnitude. This is why the original Transformer needed a careful learning-rate warmup — without it, Post-LN training is prone to divergence or requires very conservative LR at the start, because early in training the layer norm statistics themselves are still stabilizing.
In Pre-LN, the residual stream itself is never renormalized — x passes through unchanged at every layer, and only the input to each sublayer is normalized. This gives you a clean, unimpeded identity path from the first layer to the last, which is much closer to the “gradient superhighway” property that made vanilla ResNets easy to train. Pre-LN models are empirically far more robust to learning rate choice and are noticeably more forgiving of skipping or shortening warmup — which is exactly the interaction we test in the ablation below. The tradeoff is that Pre-LN networks tend to have slightly worse final performance at a given depth if warmup is properly tuned for Post-LN — Post-LN’s forced renormalization can act as an implicit regularizer once training is stable — so this isn’t a strictly-better-in-every-way swap, more a stability/performance tradeoff.


6.2 Dropout Placement
Dropout in this implementation is applied in three distinct places, each for a different reason:

After adding positional encoding to embeddings — regularizes the input representation itself.
On attention weights, inside the attention() function, after softmax — randomly zeroes out some attention connections, discouraging the model from over-relying on any single key for a given query.
On each sublayer’s output, before it’s added back to the residual stream — regularizes the update to the residual stream rather than the stream itself, which is important: dropout is never applied directly to the residual path x, only to what’s being added to it. Dropping the residual path itself would destroy the identity-mapping property that makes residual networks trainable.

7. Encoder & Decoder Stack Assembly
class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, self_attention_block, feed_forward_block, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.self_attention_block = self_attention_block
        self.feed_forward_block = feed_forward_block
        self.residual_connections = nn.ModuleList([ResidualConnection(dropout) for _ in range(2)])

    def forward(self, x, src_mask):
        x = self.residual_connections[0](x, lambda x: self.self_attention_block(x, x, x, src_mask))
        x = self.residual_connections[1](x, self.feed_forward_block)
        return x


class DecoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, self_attention_block, cross_attention_block, feed_forward_block, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.self_attention_block = self_attention_block
        self.cross_attention_block = cross_attention_block
        self.feed_forward_block = feed_forward_block
        self.residual_connections = nn.ModuleList([ResidualConnection(dropout) for _ in range(3)])

    def forward(self, x, encoder_output, src_mask, tgt_mask):
        x = self.residual_connections[0](x, lambda x: self.self_attention_block(x, x, x, tgt_mask))
        x = self.residual_connections[1](x, lambda x: self.cross_attention_block(x, encoder_output, encoder_output, src_mask))
        x = self.residual_connections[2](x, self.feed_forward_block)
        return x
Note the decoder’s cross-attention call: query = x (decoder’s own state) but key = value = encoder_output. This is exactly where the encoder’s representation of the source sequence gets injected into the decoder — the decoder is asking “given what I’ve generated so far, which parts of the source sequence are relevant right now,” and the mask used here is the src_mask (padding mask on the source), not the causal mask — causality only applies to the decoder’s self-attention over its own generated tokens.
Both encoder and decoder stacks apply a final LayerNorm after the last block, since with Pre-LN the residual stream is otherwise unnormalized all the way through — without this final norm, the output fed to the projection layer would have unbounded/unnormalized scale.

8. Training Setup

8.1 Label Smoothing
Rather than training with a hard one-hot target distribution, label smoothing spreads a small amount of probability mass (typically ε=0.1) across the non-target vocabulary:
target_distribution[correct_token] = 1 - ε
target_distribution[other_tokens] = ε / (vocab_size - 1)
This discourages the model from becoming overconfident — pushing logits to extreme values to drive the softmax output arbitrarily close to 1.0 for the correct token. Overconfidence hurts both calibration (the model’s confidence no longer reflects its actual accuracy) and, counterintuitively, BLEU-style generation metrics, since an overconfident model commits harder to early mistakes during beam search.


8.2 Learning Rate Schedule (Noam Schedule)
lr = d_model ** (-0.5) * min(step_num ** (-0.5), step_num * warmup_steps ** (-1.5))
This increases LR linearly for the first warmup_steps, then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. The warmup phase exists specifically to get past the early-training instability discussed in §6.1 — at initialization, Post-LN’s normalization statistics are not yet representative, and large early updates under a high LR can push the model into a bad region it doesn’t recover from. Warmup keeps early updates small while those statistics stabilize, then ramps up once the model is on firmer footing.


8.3 Loss Masking
Padding tokens in the target sequence must be excluded from the loss — otherwise the model is rewarded for correctly predicting <pad> after <pad>, which is a trivial, meaningless pattern that would dilute the actual training signal:
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=pad_token_id, label_smoothing=0.1)

section: 9. Ablation Study: Pre-LN vs Post-LN × Flat LR vs Warmup+Decay
text:
9. Ablation Study: Pre-LN vs Post-LN × Flat LR vs Warmup+Decay
The claim in §6.1 — that Pre-LN is more robust to LR schedule while Post-LN needs warmup — is widely repeated but worth actually testing rather than taking on faith. Setup: a 2×2 grid crossing normalization placement (Pre-LN / Post-LN) with LR schedule (flat constant LR / Noam warmup+decay), all other hyperparameters held fixed (same d_model, same number of layers/heads, same dataset, same number of steps, same seed where applicable).
Metrics tracked per cell: - Training loss curve (smoothed) - Gradient norm over time (particularly in the first few hundred steps) - Whether training diverges (loss → NaN/Inf) or plateaus early
Expected/observed pattern:









Flat LR
Warmup + Decay




Post-LN
Unstable early, high risk of divergence or requires very low flat LR to survive, which then undertrains
Stable, matches paper’s reported behavior


Pre-LN
Stable, converges reasonably even without warmup
Stable, often marginally smoother early loss curve than flat LR, but the gap to flat-LR Pre-LN is much smaller than the corresponding gap for Post-LN



The interesting result isn’t just “warmup helps” — it’s the interaction: warmup’s benefit is much larger under Post-LN than under Pre-LN. That’s the direct empirical signature of the mechanism described in §6.1 — Pre-LN’s clean identity path makes the network far less sensitive to the exact shape of the LR schedule, because gradient magnitude isn’t being repeatedly rescaled by normalization layers stacked N deep.
[Insert your actual loss curves and gradient norm plots here from the four runs.]
Takeaway: if you’re building on Pre-LN (which most modern LLMs are, including GPT-2 onward), you have more slack on LR schedule design — a reasonable warmup still helps a bit, but you’re not walking a tightrope the way the original Post-LN paper effectively was. If you’re stuck maintaining a Post-LN architecture for legacy or specific-performance reasons, the warmup schedule isn’t a nice-to-have, it’s close to a hard requirement at this depth.

10. Common Implementation Pitfalls

Forgetting the √d_model embedding scale — model still trains, but positional encoding dominates early representations, causing slower convergence.
Mask shape mismatches — attention masks need to broadcast correctly against (batch, h, seq_len, seq_len) attention score tensors; a mask shaped for a single head silently broadcasts wrong if you’re not careful with unsqueeze.
Off-by-one in decoder input/target shift — the decoder input at training time is the target sequence shifted right by one (prepended with <sos>), and the loss target is the unshifted sequence. Getting this backwards silently trains the model to copy rather than predict.
Using .view() after .transpose() without .contiguous() — covered in §4.2, raises a runtime error (or worse, silently wrong output with .reshape()).
Inconsistent dropout between train/eval — forgetting model.eval() before validation/inference leaves dropout active, adding noise to what should be deterministic generation.
Masking after softmax instead of before — leaves incorrect nonzero probability mass on masked positions unless you manually renormalize; masking with a large negative number before softmax handles this for free.

11. Results & Sanity Checks
[This section is a placeholder for your run: include a training/validation loss curve, a handful of sample translations or generations at increasing checkpoints, and 1-2 attention heatmaps — ideally one showing a head that’s learned something interpretable, like aligning source and target tokens in cross-attention.]
A useful sanity check before trusting any of the ablation results above: verify that a single attention head’s weights sum to 1 across the key dimension for every query position (post-softmax, pre-dropout), and verify that masked positions are receiving effectively zero attention weight, not just small weight. Both are easy to get subtly wrong and easy to silently ship if you don’t check.

12. Conclusion & Next Steps
Building this from scratch makes the paper’s design choices legible in a way that using nn.Transformer doesn’t — the √d_model scaling, the specific dropout placement, the Post-LN/warmup coupling, are all things you can read past in the paper but that become obvious the moment you have to get the shapes and gradients right yourself.
This is groundwork for the next few posts in this series: KV caching (which changes how self-attention is computed at inference time once you’re autoregressively decoding one token at a time), TurboQuant-style quantization, and then a shift toward flow-matching-based generative models — DiT architectures and F5-TTS specifically — where a lot of these same attention and normalization design questions resurface in a very different setting.

Code for the full implementation and the four ablation runs is available in [link to your repo].

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
There’s no shortage of transformer tutorials floating around. It’s the most basic deep learning architecture in NLP today, so why bother building one from scratch again?
Because it’s exactly that: the basic building block for almost every architecture running today. I spend my actual working hours around fast-conformer models and diffusion models, but actually building this basic transformer with my own hands (and several 2am debugging sessions) turned out to be very different and suprisingly very insightful. Enough that I decided I had to write a log about it.
So here’s that log. I built an encoder-decoder transformer straight from the original paper, trained it on opus_books for English to Italian translation, and kept a running list of every question that had me pausing mid-line wondering what the authors were thinking.
The source lives in four files: model.py for the architecture, dataset.py for the data pipeline, config.py for the hyperparameters, and train.py for the training loop. code link

section: 2. Positional Encoding: Giving the Model a Sense of Order
text:
2. Positional Encoding: Giving the Model a Sense of Order
Formulas:-
For even dimensions (\(2i\)): \[PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\frac{2i}{d_{model}}}}\right)\] For odd dimensions (\(2i + 1\)): \[PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\frac{2i}{d_{model}}}}\right)\] \(i\) is a specific feature dimension (where \(i\) goes from \(0\) to \(d_{model}/2\))






Positional Encoding: Use of sin and cos



The maths behind chosing sin and cos, it’s pros and cons and recent advancements in positional encoding is discussed in my other blog: [link: to be done]


Two implementation details:

register_buffer, not nn.Parameter: Registering in buffer allows the deterministic embeddings that never gets trained to be moved with the model across .to(device) calls and be saved/restored in state_dict().
The e^(ln(A)B) trick:  10000^(-2i/d_model) is computed as exp(-2i/d_model * ln(10000)) because torch.pow on a fractional, negative exponent across a whole tensor is less numerically stable than composing exp and log, which PyTorch has fast, stable kernels for.

\[X_{final} = \text{Dropout}\Big( E_{pos} + PE_{pos} \Big)\]

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
3. LayerNorm From Scratch






Q2: What is the use of Normalization?



As data moves non-linear activations and weight multiplications leads to Internal Covariate Shift.

The variance of the activations grows too large -> the gradients explode
It shrinks too much -> the gradients vanish
Normalization solves this by forcing the activations back to a standard scale (typically a mean of 0 and a variance of 1) at every layer. The general mathematical formula for normalization is: \[y = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma + \beta\]









Q3: Why LayerNorm and why not BatchNorm?



BatchNorm normalizes across batch dimension and assumes batch statistics are stable and representative. Two things break that assumption here:

Variable sequence lengths + padding:  Batch statistics get polluted by padding tokens that are used to fill sequences to the same length.
Batch size of 1 at inference: BatchNorm’s statistics are undefined (or at best a single noisy sample) at batch size 1.

LayerNorm is better here because it normalizes across the feature dimension (d_model) independently per token, so it behaves identically whether the batch is 1 sentence or 64.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
4. Multi-Head Attention
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]

q, k, v start as [batch, seq_len, d_model].

Then first it is converted to [batch, seq_len, h, d_k] (d_k = d_model/h)

And then transposed to[batch, h, seq_len, d_k]
WHY???? -> Allows each head to take info from all the seq tokens
After attention, .transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(...) merges the heads back. .contiguous() is required here because .transpose returns a view with non-contiguous memory, and .view() refuses to operate on that.







Q4: Why divide by √d_k? What happens if you don’t?



Assume the components of q and k are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1 (a reasonable approximation right after Xavier/careful init). The dot product q·k sums d_k such independent products, so its variance grows to Var(q·k) ≈ d_k - the standard deviation grows as √d_k.
And when passed through softmax, it is exponentiated and output collapse towards one-hot. (ex output: [0.999, 0.001, 0.000]) The gradient of softmax with respect to its logits is roughly p(1-p), which is near zero for entries pinned near 0 or 1. So your gradients completely die. Your model just sits there, learning nothing.
Dividing by √d_k renormalizes the dot product back to unit variance regardless of d_k and prevents gradient collapse.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
5. The FeedForward Block
Two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between. (512 -> 2048 -> RELU -> 512) FFN(x) = max(0, W·x + b1)W2 + b2 This block is applied pointwise.
Each token, in isolation, does its own nonlinear processing on what it just gathered.






Q5: Why is there dropout inside the FFN in modern approaches?



The dropout inside the FFN, between linear_1 and linear_2, is a modern addition.
Why it matters: d_ff is 4× d_model. Here, neurons can co-adapt (learn to always fire together to reproduce memorized patterns). A dropout is applied in the residual connection but it only acts on the compressed final output and can’t see or break up that internal co-adaptation. Internal FFN dropout regularizes the expanded space directly.







Scenario
Internal FFN dropout needed?




Small model, small d_ff
Not much, residual dropout is enough


Large model, large d_ff
Yes, co-adaptation risk grows with size


Fine-tuning on small datasets
Yes, overfitting risk is real


Large-scale pretraining
Often removed, data volume is the regularizer






Pheww !! That was a lot. But it’s not over yet. Here is the next post that starts form Residual connections (The real magic of the transformers) and goes on to explain the design choices, introduce masking and then moves onto different training nuances. link

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 6. Residual Connections: The Real Story is in the Backward Pass
text:
6. Residual Connections: The Real Story is in the Backward Pass
class ResidualConnection(nn.Module):
    '''Solves the vanishing gradient problem'''
    def __init__(self, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.dropout=nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.norm=LayerNormalisation()
    
    def forward(self, x, sublayer):
        return x+self.dropout(sublayer(self.norm(x)))

A Major change in modern approach from the 2017 paper:






Pre-LN vs Post-LN



self.norm(x) happens before sublayer(...), and the result is added to the untouched x. That’s:
\[x_{l+1} = x_l + \text{Dropout}(\text{Sub}(\text{LN}(x_l)))\]
This is Pre-LN, not the Post-LN of the original 2017 paper (LN(x + Sub(x))). Why did we do this? What is warm-up? How does it helps? Mathematical explanation and my experiment to prove it in the linked blog: [link].

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 7. Assembling the Blocks: Why Dependency Injection?
text:
7. Assembling the Blocks: Why Dependency Injection?
class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, self_attention_block: MultiHeadAttention, ff_block: FeedForwardBlock, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.self_attention_block = self_attention_block
        self.ff_block = ff_block
        self.residual_connections = nn.ModuleList([ResidualConnection(dropout) for _ in range(2)])

    def forward(self, x: Tensor, src_mask: Tensor = None):
        x = self.residual_connections[0](x, lambda x: self.self_attention_block(x, x, x, src_mask))
        x = self.residual_connections[1](x, self.ff_block)
        return x
Here we make the design choice of constructor injection for Flexibility (a custom attention variant can be swapped in) instead of the internal-init alternative which leads to tight coupling.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 9. Data Pipeline: Sentence Pairs to Padded Tensors
text:
9. Data Pipeline: Sentence Pairs to Padded Tensors
class BillingualDataset(Dataset):
    def __getitem__(self, index):
        target_pair=self.ds[index]
        src_txt=target_pair['translation'][self.src_lang]
        tgt_txt=target_pair['translation'][self.tgt_lang]

        enc_input_token=self.tokenizer_src.encode(src_txt).ids
        dec_input_token=self.tokenizer_tgt.encode(tgt_txt).ids

        enc_pad_len=self.seq_len - len(enc_input_token) - 2 # sos + eos
        dec_pad_len=self.seq_len - len(dec_input_token) - 1 # only sos OR eos, not both

        enc_input = torch.cat([self.sos_token, torch.tensor(enc_input_token, dtype=torch.int64),
                                self.eos_token, torch.tensor([self.pad_token]*enc_pad_len, dtype=torch.int64)], dim=0)

        dec_input = torch.cat([self.sos_token, torch.tensor(dec_input_token, dtype=torch.int64),
                                torch.tensor([self.pad_token]*dec_pad_len, dtype=torch.int64)], dim=0)

        label = torch.cat([torch.tensor(dec_input_token, dtype=torch.int64), self.eos_token,
                            torch.tensor([self.pad_token]*dec_pad_len, dtype=torch.int64)], dim=0)
        ...
The encoder input gets both [sos] and [eos] bookends. The decoder input only gets [sos] prepended (this is teacher forcing — the decoder is fed the shifted target sequence), while label is the same tokens shifted the other way, ending in [eos] instead of starting with [sos]. This one-position offset between dec_input and label is what turns the whole training step into “predict the next token given everything so far” — the entire autoregressive objective is encoded in this single index shift.






Knowledge point — choosing batch size



Increasing batch_size means the model updates after seeing more data per step: less noisy gradient estimates, but more compute and memory per step (with diminishing returns past a point). Smaller batches add more noise to the gradient estimate, which can act as an implicit regularizer but also makes training less stable. config.py currently sets batch_size: 8 — small enough to fit seq_len=350 comfortably, at the cost of noisier gradient estimates than a larger batch would give.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
10. Wiring It All Together
def build_transformer(src_vocab_size, tgt_vocab_size, src_seq_len, tgt_seq_len,
                       d_model=512, N=6, h=8, d_ff=2048, dropout=0.1):
    ...
    for w in transformer.parameters():
        if w.dim() > 1:
            nn.init.xavier_uniform_(w)
    return transformer
Every multi-dimensional parameter (weight matrices, not biases :- w.dim() > 1 filters those out) gets Xavier-uniform init, which scales initial weights based on fan-in/fan-out to keep activation variance roughly stable across layers at the start of training.






Knowledge point :- Xavier initialization



To calculate the ideal starting weights, Xavier initialization relies on two structural properties of the layer:

fan_in: The number of input connections (neurons) entering the layer.
fan_out: The number of output connections leaving the layer.

Depending on the distribution you choose, the weights are drawn as follows:
1. Xavier Normal Initialization Weights are drawn from a Normal (Gaussian) distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) of:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\text{fan\_in} + \text{fan\_out}}}\]
2. Xavier Uniform Initialization Weights are drawn from a Uniform distribution bounded between \([-x, x]\), where \(x\) is:
\[x = \sqrt{\frac{6}{\text{fan\_in} + \text{fan\_out}}}\]
(Note: This is commonly applied exclusively to multi-dimensional weight matrices; 1-dimensional biases are typically initialized to zero).
The Exception: It does not work well with ReLU or its variants (Leaky ReLU, GELU), because ReLU zeros out half of the distribution, cutting the variance in half. He Initialization (Kaiming initialization) works with ReLU-based networks as it adjusts the numerator to account for the dead neurons.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 11. Training Loop: Label Smoothing, Warmup, and Checkpointing
text:
11. Training Loop: Label Smoothing, Warmup, and Checkpointing
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=tokenizer_src.token_to_id('[pad]'), label_smoothing=0.1).to(device)
label_smoothing=0.1 takes some probability mass away from the “correct” token and spreads it across the rest of the vocabulary, so the model prevented from being over-confident.
ignore_index on the pad token keeps padding positions out of the loss entirely, since they carry no real supervision signal.






Q7 — What’s the point of warmup?



The paper’s Noam schedule is:
\[\text{lr} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(\text{step}^{-0.5},\ \text{step} \cdot \text{warmup}^{-1.5})\]
— linear ramp-up for the first warmup_steps, then inverse-square-root decay. Two things justify the ramp:

Adam’s moving averages start at zero. The first-and-second-moment estimates (m, v) are noisy and uninformative for the first few hundred steps regardless of architecture — a large step size applied to noisy moment estimates is how early training diverges.
It’s the direct fix for the Post-LN problem from §6. With Post-LN, late layers see much larger gradients than early layers at any fixed LR. A large LR early on lets the late layers take a big, possibly destabilizing step before the early layers — starved of usable gradient — have learned anything to make that step sensible. Warmup buys the early layers time.

Pre-LN’s identity highway (§6) makes this less critical — gradient magnitude is roughly uniform across depth from the start, so Pre-LN tolerates higher LR without warmup much better than Post-LN does. That’s the hypothesis the next section is designed to actually test rather than just assert.


train.py also handles crash recovery — config['preload'] points at a checkpoint path, and if set, model.load_state_dict, optimizer.load_state_dict, initial_epoch, and global_step are all restored before training resumes, so a training run picks up exactly where it left off rather than restarting Adam’s moment estimates from scratch.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
12. Next: A 2×2 Ablation
The architecture as written (§6) already commits to Pre-LN. The open question is how much that choice actually buys in practice, and how much of Post-LN’s instability a warmup schedule can paper over. So the plan is a 2×2:




Flat LR
Noam warmup + decay




Pre-LN
(a)
(b)


Post-LN
(c)
(d)



Hypothesis going in, straight from the §6 math: (c) should be the least stable combination — Post-LN’s gradient imbalance with no warmup cushion. (a) should be the most robust to LR choice. (d) is the original paper’s actual configuration, and should recover most of (a)’s stability despite using Post-LN. If (b) and (d) end up close, that’s evidence warmup is doing the real work; if (a) clearly beats (d), that’s evidence Pre-LN’s identity highway is doing something warmup can’t fully substitute for.
Results pending — loss curves and final BLEU/perplexity per cell go here once the four runs finish.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
Loose Threads
A couple of things that came up while reading through this code but don’t belong in the transformer itself - they’re the next two things on my list:






Knowledge point :- KV cache



Generating M new tokens with a prompt of length N naively costs O(M · (N+M)²). Caching the key/value states from previous steps drops the incremental per-token cost to O(1) relative to history length, since only the new token’s K/V needs computing.








Knowledge point :- attention memory and FlashAttention



Storing the full [B, H, S, S] attention score matrix for the backward pass is O(S²) memory. This is what makes long-context training memory-bound rather than compute-bound, and it’s exactly the problem FlashAttention is built to avoid by never materializing the full matrix.



Source: model.py, dataset.py, config.py, train.py. Architecture follows Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need” (2017), trained on the opus_books en→it dataset.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 1. Text Embeddings: Turning Tokens Into Vectors
text:
1. Text Embeddings: Turning Tokens Into Vectors
Let \(W_E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{model}}\) be the learnable embedding weight matrix.
The text embedding formula for a given token at position \(pos\) with vocabulary index \(k\) is: \[E_{pos} = W_E[k] \cdot \sqrt{d_{model}}\]
nn.Embedding is just a lookup table: [vocab_size, d_model], initialized randomly and learned during training. During forward pass :- [batch, seq_len] -> [batch, seq_len, d_model]






Q1: Why multiply by √d_model?



The positional encodings (next section) have values bounded in [-1, 1]. Raw embeddings, especially right after Xavier init, sit at a much smaller scale.
√d_model scale-up the text embeddings that becomes comparable to the additive positional signal early in training.

title: Pre-LN vs Post-LN, warmup, and the identity highway
text:
Post-LN (x_{l+1} = LN(x_l + Sub(x_l))): every backward gradient must pass through every LayerNorm Jacobian in the stack, in sequence. That Jacobian zeroes the gradient’s component along the mean direction, zeroes the component along the (x-μ)/σ direction (scale invariance), and shrinks whatever’s left by ≤ 1/σ. Multiply N of these together and you get exponential gradient shrinkage with depth — subspaces that survive one layer’s projection can get killed by the next.
Loss → [J_LN] → [J_LN] → [J_LN] → ... → [J_LN] → Early layer weights
        Layer N   Layer N-1                 Layer 1
        (shrinks) (shrinks again)          (barely anything left)
Pre-LN (x_{l+1} = x_l + Sub(LN(x_l))): the residual x_l is added outside the LN, so
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_l} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_{l+1}} \cdot \left(I + J_{\text{Sub}} \cdot J_{\text{LN}}\right)\]
The identity term I is a direct gradient highway: a copy of the output gradient reaches every layer untouched, no matter what the sublayer Jacobian does to the other term.
Loss
 │
 ├─────────────────────── Identity highway ──────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                    │
[Sub·LN Jacobian] → [Sub·LN Jacobian] → ... → [Sub·LN Jacobian]      │
                                                                      │
                                                        Early weights ←┘


Because Post-LN gradients shrink with depth, different layers have wildly different gradient magnitudes at any given step — a single global LR has to serve all of them at once:



Learning rate
Late layers
Early layers




Too high
Explode → divergence
Still okay


Too low
Learn slowly
Learn essentially nothing


Just right
Marginal stability
Still barely learning



There is no single LR that keeps late layers stable and gives early layers a usable signal — this is precisely why the original paper needs a warmup schedule as a bandage (more on that in §11). Pre-LN’s identity highway keeps gradient magnitude roughly uniform across depth, so one LR works comfortably almost everywhere, and higher LRs become tolerable.
The trade-off: Pre-LN’s residual stream grows unboundedly in the forward pass (nothing renormalizes it layer to layer), which is exactly why Encoder and Decoder each end with one more LayerNormalisation() after the last block — a final cleanup norm that Post-LN doesn’t strictly need, since Post-LN already renormalizes at every layer.
class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layers: nn.ModuleList):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers=layers
        self.norm=LayerNormalisation()   # <- the Pre-LN "final cleanup" norm
    
    def forward(self, x: Tensor, mask: Tensor=None):
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, mask)
        return self.norm(x)
That final self.norm(x) isn’t decorative — it’s the tell that confirms this implementation committed to Pre-LN, and it’s required for Pre-LN to work correctly.

section: Honourable mentions: Dropout layers in transformers (They are everywhere !!!)
text:
Honourable mentions: Dropout layers in transformers (They are everywhere !!!)
While writting the code, I found we were using dropout in every next layer. So I set out to understand it’s implementation and use of every single dropout.

1. After Positional Encoding
Applied on the sum of token embeddings + positional encodings.
Forces the model not to over-rely on any specific position or embedding dimension right from the start - regularizes the input before it enters the encoder/decoder stack.

Paper (Section 5.4): “we apply dropout to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings.”




2. On Attention Weights (inside Attention block)
Applied after softmax, before multiplying by V.
After softmax, each row is a probability distribution over all tokens. Without dropout, the model can memorize which tokens to always attend to (attention collapse). Dropout randomly zeroes out weights, forcing the model to spread attention and learn more robust, distributed patterns.



3. In Residual Connection block (On Sublayer Output)
def forward(self, x, sublayer):
    return x + self.dropout(sublayer(self.norm(x)))
Applied on the output of each sublayer (Attention or FeedForward), before adding back to the residual stream.
The sublayer output is the new information being added to the residual stream
Dropping parts of it forces the model not to rely too heavily on any single transformation

Paper: “We apply dropout to the output of each sub-layer, before it is added to the sub-layer input.”




4. Inside FeedForward - Between the Two Linear Layers (Modern Addition)
def forward(self, x):
    x = F.relu(self.linear1(x))   # d_model → d_ff
    x = self.dropout(x)            # NOT in original paper
    x = self.linear2(x)            # d_ff → d_model
    return x
Not in the original paper - added in modern implementations.
The FFN expands to 4× the model size internally (d_ff = 4 × d_model).
In this large intermediate space, neurons can co-adapt - always firing together to produce memorized patterns.
The Residual Connection’s dropout acts on the final compressed output and cannot prevent co-adaptation forming inside the FFN. Internal dropout breaks this by regularizing the expanded space directly.

Full Dropout Flow
Token IDs
    │
[Text Encoding]               ← no dropout
    │
    + [Positional Encoding]
    │
[Dropout] ◄─────────────────── #1: input representation
    │

│                                  │

│      │                           │
│  [Attention]                     │
│      │                           │
│  [Dropout] ◄─────────────────── #2: attention weights (inside Attention)
│      │                           │

│      │                           │
│   x + sublayer(x)               │
│                                  │
│  (same structure for FFN layer)  │
│                                  │

│                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────┘

Hyperparameter
All dropout locations share the same p value:

Base model: p = 0.1
Large model: p = 0.3

It is a single hyperparameter tuned across the entire architecture.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
text:
Loose Threads
A couple of things that came up while reading through this code but don’t belong in the transformer itself - they’re the next two things on my list:






Knowledge point :- KV cache



Generating M new tokens with a prompt of length N naively costs O(M · (N+M)²). Caching the key/value states from previous steps drops the incremental per-token cost to O(1) relative to history length, since only the new token’s K/V needs computing.








Knowledge point :- attention memory and FlashAttention



Storing the full [B, H, S, S] attention score matrix for the backward pass is O(S²) memory. This is what makes long-context training memory-bound rather than compute-bound, and it’s exactly the problem FlashAttention is built to avoid by never materializing the full matrix.



Source: Github repo
